adds.title: Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: HRW's state-by-state map of transgender rights in Mexico shows Veracruz was among the last states to legislate: only in 2025 did its congress reform the Civil Code to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, with no age requirement. The page documents no prison-placement rule for Veracruz and no information on where trans prisoners are housed; its Veracruz content concerns identity documents (civil registry) only.

records.note: No source was found documenting where transgender prisoners are housed in Veracruz. Wikipedia full-text search ('transgender prisoner Veracruz') returned no relevant article. A State Department 2023 human-rights report page for Mexico was fetched but returned no extractable text (JS shell), so it could not be verified and is not cited. The only Veracruz-specific gender-identity law found (HRW map) is the 2025 civil-code legal-gender-recognition reform, which concerns documents, not prison placement. The housing datum for this record therefore remains a gap: placement would fall under Mexico's national penal-execution framework of sex-based facility classification, but no Veracruz-specific verified source on trans-prisoner housing was obtained in this lane.

adds.title: World Report 2024: Mexico | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: HRW World Report 2024, Mexico chapter: documents Mexico's national legal-gender-recognition framework (administrative name/gender-marker changes on birth certificates in 21 of 32 states, a 2019 Supreme Court ruling setting LGR standards, extended to adolescents and children in March 2022). Its SOGI section covers marriage and document-level recognition only and contains no information on where transgender prisoners are housed in Oaxaca or in Mexico generally.

adds.title: Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: HRW's state-by-state map documents that Oaxaca created an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure in 2019, extended it to children 12 and older in 2021, and saw a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling reopen access for children under 12. As with Veracruz, the page contains no prison-placement data: Oaxaca's only documented gender-identity law concerns identity documents, not where trans inmates are held.

records.note: No source was found documenting where transgender prisoners are housed in Oaxaca. Wikipedia full-text search ('transgender prisoner Oaxaca') returned no relevant article (only tangential hits on muxe culture and LGBTQ history). HRW World Report 2024's Mexico chapter, fetched for this record, contains no trans-prisoner content. Oaxaca's documented gender-identity law is administrative legal gender recognition (2019, extended 2021 and 2023) — documents, not placement. The housing datum for Oaxaca therefore remains a gap: no verified source on facility placement of trans inmates in the state was obtained in this lane.
